Pulsed Electroreduction of CO2 on Cu-Ag Alloy Electrodes S. Ishimaru,z R. Shiratsuchi, and G. Nogami
Department of Electrical Engineering, Kyushu Institute of Technology, Kitakyushu 804-8550, Japan
Highly selective reduction of CO2 to C2 compounds such as CH3CHO, C2H5OH, and C2H4 has been achieved on CuAg alloy electrodes by pulsed electroreduction. The faradaic efficiencies of C2 compounds produced on CuAg alloy electrodes were varied with the atomic ratio of Cu to Ag. The total value of faradaic efficiencies for these C2 compounds was 54.2% for the pulsed electroreduction on a CuAg alloy electrode (Cu/Ag = 28/72) with an anodic bias of Va 5 20.4 V and a cathodic bias of Vc 5 22.0 V vs. Ag/AgCl. It was found that the formation of an oxide layer on Cu and the desorption of intermediates on Ag under anodic bias were key factors for the selective reduction of CO2 to C2 compounds on CuAg alloy electrodes. © 2000 The Electrochemical Society. Some reports suggest the possibility of selective synthesis of oxygenates such as alcohols and aldehydes by electrochemical reduction on copper oxide,1 conductive oxide mixture,2 and copper3 electrodes. We have proposed a new electrolysis technique for electrochemical reduction of CO2, applying an anodic bias (Va) and a cathodic bias (Vc) alternatively. The employment of the pulsed method to electrochemical reduction of CO2 was more effective in selectivity than that of static electroreductions such as galvano- and potentiostatic electrolyses.4,5 In Ref. 4 and 5, we pointed out that the selectivity of reduction products was due to the change in the concentration of proton or adsorbed hydrogen atoms and the formation of an oxide layer on electrode surfaces during the anodic period. On a pure Ag electrode, it is known that the main product of the static electroreduction of CO2 is CO.
6,7 Meanwhile, we investigated pulsed electroreduction which mainly synthesizes hydrocarbons as well as on the Cu electrodes.8 Recently, Saito et al. indicated that a part of this effect on the Ag electrode might be ascribed to Cu metal adhered to Ag electrode surface.9 However, the production of hydrocarbon for the pulsed electroreduction of CO2 on pure Ag metal electrode should not be due to Cu adhered onto the Ag surface. This result should be attributed to interactions between Cu and Ag. Therefore, the pulsed electroreduction on the alloyed Cu and Ag electrodes might favor the formation of hydrocarbons and oxygenates.
In this paper, the pulsed electroreduction of CO2 on the alloy electrodes having various atomic ratios of Cu to Ag was investigated, especially, the selectivity for the production of C2 compounds such as C2H4, C2H5OH, and CH3CHO were studied.

sections.heading: Experimental
sections.text:
The copper (99.999%) and silver (99.99%) metals to be used for the preparation of CuAg alloy electrodes were purchased from Nilaco Co. Ltd. The CuAg alloy electrodes with four different atomic ratios of (Cu/Ag), 87/13, 55/45, 28/72, and 13/87 were prepared by melting Cu and Ag metals by means of a microwave inductive furnace in an Ar atmosphere. The procedure of the pulsed electroreduction, analytical methods, and the equipment of electrolysis are described in Ref. 4. Cathodic period (Tc) and anodic period (Ta) in the pulsed reduction were both set at 5 s.
All potentials were referred to the Ag/AgCl electrode. Electroreduction of CO2 was performed for 8 h in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 buffer solution (pH 6.8) at 108C.
All measurements were performed in a conventional H-type gastight glass cell. A platinum counter electrode was separated from the working electrode compartment by an ion exchange membrane (Nafion 417). A gas chromatograph (Yanaco G-3810) was equipped with a thermally conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID). Molecular sieve of 5 A and Porapak Q were used for CO and H2 analysis in the TCD and CH4 and C2H4 analysis in the FID, respectively. Soluble products such as CH3CHO and C2H5OH

sections.heading: Results
sections.text:
The pulsed electroreductions of CO2 were performed over the cathodic bias between Vc 5 22.5 and 21.75 V while the anodic bias between Va 5 20.9 and 0.25 V. Figures 1, 2, and 3 show the faradaic efficiencies h for CH4, CO, and HCOOH, respectively, as a function of Va on CuAg alloy electrodes, with different atomic ratios, and pure metal (Cu and Ag) electrodes; cathodic bias were kept constant at Vc 5 22.25 V. It was found that these faradaic efficiencies depended on the atomic ratio of Cu/Ag. For the pulsed reduction, h(CH4) on the pure Cu electrode was more than 10% over the applied anodic bias Va, reaching a maximum at Va 5 20.25 V. On the pure Ag electrode, the main product was CO in the static electroreduction,6,7 and CH4 in the pulsed electroreduction in a limited potential range of Va 5 20.6 to 20.4 V. As apparent from Fig. 1 and 2, h(CH4) and h(CO) on the pure Ag electrode show opposite characteristics. After the pulsed electroreduction, no trace of Ag and Cu in electrolytes could be detected by an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) emission spectroscopy (Shimadzu ICPS-8000), implying that the dissolution of electrodes did not occur during the pulsed electroreduction.
Products on the counter electrode were also determined by the gas chromatograph and the ion chromatograph. No products could be traced except oxygen. It was confirmed that only oxygen evolution took place at counter electrode during electroreduction.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text:
It was found that the pulsed electroreduction of CO2 on CuAg alloy electrodes showed higher faradaic efficiencies for the production of C2 compounds, such as C2H4, C2H5OH, and CH3CHO, than that of the pure Cu and Ag metal electrodes. A similar increase in the yields of C2H4 have been observed by Nakato et al.
10 for a potentiostatic electrolysis of CO2 on alloyed CuAg electrodes. It may be suggested that there are some advantages in the formation of the C2 compounds on the CuAg electrode. For the pulsed electroreduction on the Cu electrode, the formation of the C2 compounds was preferred to that of CH4. In previous work, it was found that the increase in the C2 compounds for the Cu electrode was due to the formation of an oxide layer on the electrode surface.5 It is natural to consider from the standard reduction potential for Ag2O that the formation of an oxide layer on Ag electrode should not occur for the applied bias range between Va 5 20.7 and 20.4 V vs. Ag/AgCl. Therefore, it can be concluded that the production mechanism of C2 compounds on the Ag electrode might differ from that on the Cu electrode. In the
case of ordinary static electrochemical reductions of CO2 in aqueous solutions, Ag give CO as the main product. Recently, Oda et al. reported that the desorption of CO occurred above ca. 20.5 V on a Ag electrode.11 In the pulsed electroreduction on the Ag electrode, the productions of alcohol and hydrocarbon were observed when the anodic bias was set between 20.6 and 20.3 V. Therefore the production mechanism of C2 compounds on the Ag electrode may be related to the desorption reactions of CO and the adsorption of the hydrogen atom in the cathodic period. On the other hand, on the Cu electrode, it was inferred that the desorption of CO would not occur over the anodic period with such a range of Va between 20.7 and 20.4 V as reported by Oda et al. Therefore, in the anodic periods of the pulsed electroreduction of CO2 on CuAg alloy electrodes, the desorption of CO on the Ag surface takes place, while the surface CO does not desorb on the Cu surface. Thus, there may be a possibility of controlling the quantity of the adsorbed CO on the electrode surface by changing the atomic ratio of Cu to Ag. Adsorbed CO on the electrode surface could affect the reaction processes for the reduction of CO2 during the following cathodic period.
DeWulf et al. proposed the existence of surface formyl (e.g., CuCHO) and surface carbene (e.g., Cu 5 CH2) species, which were intermediates in the reduction of CO2 on Cu electrode.
12 The surface carbene species can form CH4 on reaction with hydrogen atoms. The dimerization reaction of the surface carbene species can lead to the formation of C2H4. On the other hand, Sammells and Cook proposed another scheme for the formation of C2H4, which was accompanied by a reaction between the surface CO species and the surface carbene species.13 A series of the reactions between the surface CO species, the surface carbene species, and adsorbed hydrogen atoms

produce acetaldehyde and ethanol in the first step reaction and the second step reaction, respectively. In further reduction, the formation of C2H4 will occur. Judging from the similarity of the curves of h(C2H4), h(C2H5OH), and h(CH3CHO) as shown in Fig. 4, the formation of the C2 compounds may proceed in the scheme proposed by Sammells and Cook.
The optimum anodic bias of the yield of CH4 and the C2 compounds was 20.45 and 20.55 V as shown in Fig. 3 and 4, respectively. In static electroreduction of CO2 in aqueous solutions, the yields of CH4 and C2H4 depend on the local pH on the electrode surface.3 Therefore, the difference in the optimum Va for CH4 and C2 compounds should be due to the difference in the concentration of hydrogen atoms adsorbed on the electrode surface, namely, due to the difference in the quantity of hydrogen atoms desorbed in the anodic period. The formation of carbon by the reaction between desorbed CO and hydrogen atoms was promoted at ca. Va 5 20.45 V. In the meanwhile, the desorbed CO might be maintained because of lower concentration of atomic hydrogen desorbed at ca. Va 5 20.55 V. In the latter case, the dimerization reaction between CO and CH2 would be promoted during the anodic period.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
The selective production of C2 compounds has proved to be partly possible by using the CuAg alloy electrodes in the pulsed electroreduction of CO2. In the previous paper,
8 it was reported that the applied anodic bias was an important parameter for the production of hydrocarbon and the selectivity of reduction products because of the forma-

tion of an oxide layer and desorption of adsorbed hydrogen atoms. In addition, it has been found that the desorption of the intermediate CO species during the cathodic period is also an important factor. At the more positive Va, i.e. Va > 20.6 V, the desorption of the intermediate CO species formed during the cathodic period will occur from a part of the Ag metal and will not occur from a part of Cu metal. The preferential production of the C2 compounds on CuAg alloy electrodes is caused by the difference of adsorption between the Cu and Ag metal.
